title: A loop that never starts
summary: Learn why a loop can compile but run zero times when its starting value already makes the condition false.
objectives: Explain when a `for` loop sets its starting value and checks its condition.
Trace a loop to find out whether its body runs at all.
Choose a starting value that matches the loop condition.
Recognise loop initialisation mistakes in counting loops and array loops.

blocks.text: A loop can look ready to count, but never run its body. This happens when its starting value already makes its condition false. In this example, `i` starts at 5, but the loop asks whether `i` is less than 3.

bad.title: Starts too high, so the body never runs

good.title: Starts at 0, so the body runs three times

blocks.note: Both programs compile. Java does not reject the first loop: it checks `5 < 3`, gets `false`, and skips the body. The mistake shows up when the program runs, not at compile time.

blocks.text: In a `for` loop, the initialisation sets the counter before the first condition check. Initialisation runs exactly once. If the condition is false at that first check, the body is skipped. The update, such as `i++`, only happens after the body, so it cannot fix a bad starting value.

blocks.caption: A `for` loop checks its condition before it runs the body
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[Set counter once]
  B --> C{Condition true?}
  C -- yes --> D[Run body]
  D --> E[Update counter]
  E --> C
  C -- no --> F([Leave loop])

blocks.title: Check the first test
blocks.text: Before tracing all the passes, put the starting value into the condition. If the condition is already false, the loop runs zero times.

sections.title: Trace it, one step at a time

blocks.text: Trace the broken loop by writing down its starting value and testing the condition before imagining any output. The body runs only when that first test is true.

blocks.caption: Tracing `for (int i = 5; i < 3; i++)`
rows: Skip the body and leave the loop

blocks.text: There is no update and no pass through the body. For comparison, if the loop starts at 0, the tests are `0 < 3`, `1 < 3`, `2 < 3`, and then `3 < 3`. The first three are true, so the body runs three times.

blocks.caption: How many times the body runs with a condition of `i < 3`

blocks.text: In each example, first compare the starting value with the condition. Then check that the update moves the counter in a direction that can eventually make the condition false.

bad.title: Counting upward, but starting past the end

good.title: Start at 1 to count up to 3

blocks.note: For the bad version, the first test is `4 < 4`, which is false. For the fixed version, `1 < 4` is true, and the loop counts 1, 2 and 3.

bad.title: Counting down, but starting below the target

good.title: Start at 3 to count down to 1

blocks.note: For the bad version, the first test is `0 > 1`, which is false. A countdown that uses `i > 0` needs to start above 0. Starting at 3 lets the body run for 3, 2 and 1.

blocks.text: The condition and the starting value have to agree. These examples look different, but each loop skips its body because the first condition check is false.

bad.title: An array loop starts at its length

good.title: Start array traversal at 0

blocks.note: In the bad version, `i < values.length` is false from the start. Array traversal normally starts at 0 because array positions start at 0.

bad.title: A countdown starts below the condition

blocks.note: The bad version fails its first test because `-1 > 0` is false. The good version starts at 2, so the condition is true at first.

blocks.title: A different initialisation mistake
blocks.text: An accumulator is a total that grows as values are added. Initialise it before the loop. If you write `int sum = 0;` inside the body, it resets on every pass. That is a different bug, but it is also caused by putting initialisation in the wrong place.

blocks.question: How many times does this loop print?
blocks.explanation: The first test is `6 < 4`, which is false. The body runs zero times.

blocks.question: Which starting value makes this loop print 1, 2 and 3?
blocks.explanation: Starting at 1 makes the tests true for 1, 2 and 3. When `i` reaches 4, `i < 4` is false and the loop stops.

blocks.question: Why does this loop run zero times?
options: The first condition check is false
The update happens before the first condition check
Java always skips a loop body once
blocks.explanation: The first test is `0 > 0`, which is false. The loop compiles, but its body is skipped when the program runs.

items: A `for` loop runs its initialisation once, before its first condition check.
If the first condition check is false, the body runs zero times.
Check the starting value in the condition before tracing any updates.
Choose a starting value that matches the direction and condition of the loop.
A loop that never starts usually compiles; the mistake shows when the program runs.
